geo_headlines: THE NASDAQ 100 SET ANOTHER RECORD; THE 10-YEAR HIT ITS HIGHEST CLOSE SINCE 2002. The Nasdaq 100 rose 0.87% Monday to 31,076.44, above Friday's record on both the close and the intraday high, and the Nasdaq Composite closed at a record 27,477.31 (+1.05%), led by Nvidia (+2.1%). The S&P 500 rose 0.66% to 7,773.95, 0.32% below its August 13 record. **The 10-year Treasury closed at 5.31%, its highest close since May 2002, after trading above 5.35% intraday.**

OIL SLIPPED BELOW $100. Brent December is $98.31 (-2.0%) and WTI November $87.75 (-1.9%), after Monday settles of $100.32 and $89.43. Saudi Aramco cut its November Arab Light price for Asia to $5 below the benchmark, a six-year low (Rigzone, citing Bloomberg), and Middle East exports outside Iran passed prewar levels last week (AFP). Aramco's CEO warned the supply cushion is "scarily thin."

IRAN: TRUMP SAYS THE WAR IS 'ESSENTIALLY ALMOST OVER'. Trump called higher gas prices "a small price to pay" (Iran International). Iran's President Pezeshkian called talks with the US meaningless. A tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz Monday after two were hit Sunday (UKMTO). The US moved B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford over a suspected Iranian drone threat (Wall Street Journal, via the Independent).

SERVICES COOLED, BUT PRICES DID NOT. ISM services slipped to 54.9 from 55.4, about in line with forecasts; prices paid rose to 74.0, the highest since 2022 (TheStreet). FedWatch now puts an October hike at 23.2%, from 21.0% Friday; December 85.2%.

FUTURES UP, ASIA MOSTLY HIGHER. S&P 500 futures 7,850 (+0.30%) and Nasdaq 100 futures 31,451.50 (+0.43%) as of 6:55 AM ET. The Nikkei closed up 1.1% at 70,683.98 and Hong Kong rose 0.8%; Seoul fell 0.9% (AP, AFP). London, Paris and Frankfurt opened higher, with the FTSE 100 up 0.5% (AFP). Gold $4,188.10 (+0.8%).

TODAY: TRADE DATA AND THREE FED SPEAKERS. August trade balance at 8:30 (BEA). New York Fed President Williams at 9:05, Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman at 10:45 and Kansas City Fed President Schmid at 1:15. Constellation Brands reports. FOMC minutes Wednesday at 2:00 PM.
client_frame_short: Two things are true at once. Stocks keep climbing: the Nasdaq 100 set another record Monday and futures are up again this morning. **But the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.31%, its highest close since 2002, so borrowing costs keep rising even as stocks rally.** Oil is helping, now back below $100 as Gulf exports recover. For clients, this is the trade-off of a strong economy with sticky inflation: stocks are earning their keep, and bonds now pay more than they have in a generation. Nothing here calls for changes; the next test is the Fed minutes Wednesday.
client_frame:
If a client calls this morning, the story is stocks and bonds telling different stories.

Stocks: the Nasdaq 100 closed at a record Monday for the second straight session, led by chip and AI companies. The S&P 500 is within half a percent of its August record. Futures are up again this morning.

Bonds: the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.31%, the highest since May 2002. Long rates are rising faster than short ones. That pattern usually means investors want more pay to hold long bonds, because of inflation and heavy government borrowing, not because they expect the Fed to keep raising rates. Fed hike odds for October are still only about one in four.

Inflation: the service sector kept growing in September, but the prices businesses pay rose to their highest level since 2022. That is why yields have not fallen even after a weak jobs report.

Oil: Brent fell back below $100. Saudi Arabia cut its prices to Asian buyers, and Gulf exports are recovering toward prewar levels. President Trump said the Iran war is "essentially almost over," though Iran's president called talks meaningless and tankers are still being hit.

Why it matters: higher long rates raise mortgage costs and make bonds more competitive with stocks. So far, earnings optimism around AI has outweighed that pressure, but it leaves less room for disappointment.

This week: three Fed officials speak today, the minutes of the September meeting come out Wednesday, and consumer sentiment arrives Friday.

For clients, the message holds: high-quality bonds pay more than 5% for a decade, an opportunity to lock in income, and long-term equity plans do not need changing. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40% (now 5.31%), a 30-year above 5.75% (now 5.66%), or a resumption of US strikes on Iran that sends Brent well above $105.
